summary: Specifies additional RADIUS attributes for IPv6 in residential broadband deployments. They are used for authorization and accounting and allow assigning host addresses, DNS server addresses, routes and named delegated prefix pools.

plainLanguage.summary: New fields on a membership form for how the network hands out addresses, directions and neighborhood blocks to customers' home equipment.

questions: how does radius assign ipv6 addresses
how does radius assign ipv6 dns servers
subtitle: Five new RADIUS attributes that let an authentication server hand out IPv6 addresses, DNS servers, routes and pool names to broadband customers.

tldr.problem: RADIUS could already carry some IPv6 information, but residential broadband networks also need per-user control of DHCPv6 addresses, DNS servers, announced routes and named address or prefix pools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five RADIUS attributes (types 168 to 172) that the RADIUS server sends to the network access server, which then uses DHCPv6 or Router Advertisements to pass the information on to the customer's gateway or host.
tldr.outcome: The attributes are a Proposed Standard, work for both authorization and accounting, and need no special handling in Diameter. They inherit the known security weaknesses of RADIUS.

today: RFC 6911 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The five attributes it defines remain the definition of these RADIUS types.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6911 specifies additional RADIUS attributes that support configuring DHCPv6 and ICMPv6 Router Advertisement (RA) parameters on a per-user basis. They complement the attributes already defined in RFC 3162 and RFC 4818.

The document lists five goals: assigning specific IPv6 addresses to hosts via DHCPv6, assigning an IPv6 DNS server address, configuring more specific routes announced through the Route Information Option of RFC 4191, assigning a named delegated prefix pool for DHCPv6 prefix delegation (RFC 3633), and assigning a named stateful address pool for DHCPv6 address assignment (RFC 3315).
sections.plainLanguage: The network already had a way to tell the front desk some things about each customer. This RFC adds five new notes the office can send, all about how a customer gets set up on the newer kind of internet address.

sections.title: The Deployment Scenario
sections.content:
The typical scenario has four parts: an IP routing Residential Gateway (RG) or host, a Layer 2 Access Node (AN) such as a DSLAM, an IP Network Access Server (NAS) that includes the AAA client, and a AAA server. The RADIUS conversation runs between the NAS and the AAA server.

The NAS may use an address configuration protocol such as DHCPv6 to serve the RG or host. The RADIUS server authenticates each RG or host and returns the attributes used for authorization and accounting. These can include a host's IPv6 address, a DNS server address and a set of routes to advertise through a suitable protocol such as ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery. The name of a prefix pool for DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation, or of an address pool for DHCPv6 address assignment, can also come from the AAA server.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer's home box talks to a local front desk, and the front desk checks with the central office. The office's answer says what the front desk should give out.

sections.title: Addresses and DNS Servers
sections.content:
Framed-IPv6-Address (type 168) carries one 128-bit IPv6 address that is assigned to the NAS-facing interface of the RG or host. It MAY appear in Access-Accept packets and MAY appear several times. In an Access-Request it MAY serve as a hint of the address the NAS would prefer, but the server need not honor it. The NAS is assumed to add a route for the address, so the server does not also need to send a host Framed-IPv6-Route attribute for it. The attribute has length 18.

RFC 3162 already allowed an address through Framed-Interface-Id plus Framed-IPv6-Prefix, but that split suits PPP better than DHCPv6, and a single attribute makes accounting records easier to process. To avoid ambiguity when all three appear together, Framed-IPv6-Address is meant for DHCPv6-assigned addresses, while Framed-IPv6-Prefix and Framed-Interface-Id cover addresses assigned through SLAAC.

DNS-Server-IPv6-Address (type 169, length 18) holds the address of a DNS server. It MAY be included several times in an Access-Accept. Its content can be copied into the DHCPv6 DNS Recursive Name Server Option (RFC 3646) or the Router Advertisement Recursive DNS Server Option (RFC 6106). When several are present, the addresses SHOULD be copied in the order received.
sections.plainLanguage: One note says which exact address a customer gets. Another says which directory service to ask for names. If there are several directories, they keep the same order.

sections.title: Route Information
sections.content:
Route-IPv6-Information (type 170) specifies a prefix, and the matching route, for the user on the NAS. The NAS announces it using the Route Information Option from RFC 4191 or an equivalent method. Other details such as preference or lifetime are left to the NAS, for example through local configuration.

The attribute has a Reserved byte, an 8-bit Prefix-Length from 0 to 128, and a variable Prefix field. The Length is at least 4 and no larger than 20. The prefix field is 0, 8, or 16 octets depending on Length, and bits past the prefix length MUST be zero.

The RFC explains why existing attributes are not enough. Framed-IPv6-Prefix can be advertised in an RA but cannot configure more specific routes. Framed-IPv6-Route configures a route on the NAS, but it does not cause the route to be announced in an RA.
sections.plainLanguage: This note tells the front desk to announce a particular road to the customer's home. The older notes could either point to a big area or set up a road at the desk, but not announce a specific road to the customer.

sections.title: Named Pools
sections.content:
Delegated-IPv6-Prefix-Pool (type 171) carries the name of a pool that SHOULD be used to pick an IPv6 delegated prefix for the user. It is for a NAS acting as a DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation server (RFC 3633). Stateful-IPv6-Address-Pool (type 172) names the pool that SHOULD be used to pick an address for DHCPv6 stateful addressing, as an alternative to sending explicit addresses with Framed-IPv6-Address.

Both use a string field whose Length is at least 3. The string is not NULL terminated, and it names a pool configured on the NAS. If the NAS does not support pools of that kind, it MUST ignore the attribute. Both MAY be sent in an Access-Request as a hint that the server need not honor.

To avoid ambiguity when prefix delegation and SLAAC share a network, Delegated-IPv6-Prefix-Pool is restricted to prefix pools used in DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation, and Framed-IPv6-Pool is used for SLAAC prefix pools.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of naming one exact house number, the office can say which street to pick from. If the front desk has no such street, it ignores the note.

sections.title: Packet Usage and Diameter
sections.content:
A table in the RFC shows where each attribute may appear. In Access-Request, Access-Accept and Accounting-Request packets each may appear zero or more times (0+), and none may appear in Access-Reject or Access-Challenge. The optional presence in requests lets a NAS give the server a hint in advance, which may help when a user reconnects or has a static address. The server is under no obligation to honor such hints.

The attributes are allocated from the standard RADIUS type space, so Diameter entities need no special handling.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes can go on the request form, the approval, and the usage report, but never on a rejection. If the desk makes a suggestion, the office may say no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RADIUS may run over IPv4 or IPv6 in these networks, and the known security vulnerabilities of the RADIUS protocol apply to the new attributes. The RFC cites an analysis of the RADIUS authentication protocol for those weaknesses.

A trust relationship between the NAS and the RADIUS server is expected to be in place, with communication optionally secured by IPsec or Transport Layer Security (RFC 6614).
sections.plainLanguage: The new notes are only as safe as the old way of sending notes. The desk and the office should already trust each other, and can lock their messages for extra safety.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned five new RADIUS attribute types in the Radius Attribute Types registry: Framed-IPv6-Address (168), DNS-Server-IPv6-Address (169), Route-IPv6-Information (170), Delegated-IPv6-Prefix-Pool (171) and Stateful-IPv6-Address-Pool (172).
sections.plainLanguage: Each new note got its own official number so everyone recognizes it.

items.label: Framed-IPv6-Address
items.desc: One DHCPv6-assigned IPv6 address for the RG or host.

items.label: DNS-Server-IPv6-Address
items.desc: IPv6 address of a DNS server.

items.label: Route-IPv6-Information
items.desc: A prefix and route to announce to the host.

items.label: Delegated-IPv6-Prefix-Pool
items.desc: Name of a pool for DHCPv6 prefix delegation.

items.label: Stateful-IPv6-Address-Pool
items.desc: Name of a pool for DHCPv6 stateful addressing.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: In bytes; at least 4 and no larger than 20.

fields.name: Prefix-Length
fields.desc: Number of leading valid bits, 0 to 128.
